label: Prop 1
title: Housing and veterans bond
official: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
short: Borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing and veterans' home loans.
what: Lets the state sell $11.25 billion in [[go-bond|general obligation bonds]]. About $10 billion goes to state housing programs, mostly affordable rental housing. The other $1.25 billion funds Cal-Vet home loans for veterans, which the veterans repay.
yes: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
no: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
fiscal: $500–600 million a year from the [[general-fund|General Fund]] for about 25 years to repay the bonds.
short_term: Money becomes available to housing programs as bonds are sold over several years.
long_term: About $500–600 million a year of state budget goes to repayment for roughly 25 years. The LAO estimates the money could subsidize up to 40,000 rental units.
supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services
pro: Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers—teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
deep: Allocation of the $10 billion for state programs: $7.2 billion affordable multifamily rental housing (including $150 million for youth housing); $1.1 billion homeownership assistance; $500 million infrastructure; $450 million farmworker housing; $350 million UC and CSU student housing; $200 million tribal housing; $200 million local pilot programs.
The $1.25 billion veterans' share is repaid by veterans' loan payments. The LAO notes those payments have always covered what is owed on past Cal-Vet bonds.
"No new taxes" is accurate, and the bonds are still repaid from existing General Fund revenue, about a quarter of one percent of the budget each year.
Combined with Prop 38, the two bonds would cost about $1 billion a year in General Fund repayment.

money.yesNote: Two carpenters' councils, Airbnb, and Building a Better California ($1M each); Meta's California committee ($0.6M); Anthropic ($0.5M)

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Will Prop 1 raise my taxes?
faq.a: No. It creates no new tax. The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from its existing [[general-fund|General Fund]], about $500–600 million a year for about 25 years. That is roughly a quarter of 1% of the state budget. Because of interest, the total cost is about 15% more (after inflation) than paying up front.

faq.q: Who is the housing for?
faq.a: Mostly lower-income Californians. The largest share, $7.2 billion, goes to rental housing, where units generally must be reserved for low-income households for 55 years. Another $1.1 billion helps low- and moderate-income first-time buyers. Smaller amounts go to farmworker housing, UC and CSU student housing, tribal housing, and veterans' home loans.

faq.q: How much housing would it pay for?
faq.a: The LAO estimates subsidies for up to 40,000 rental apartments, about 2,500 farmworker units, and about 1,200 student beds. It would also help up to 40,000 households become or stay homeowners, including about 2,100 veterans. The bond money is usually combined with other government funding.

faq.q: Does the veterans' part cost taxpayers?
faq.a: Not directly. The $1.25 billion for Cal-Vet home loans is repaid by veterans' monthly loan payments. The LAO says those payments have always covered what the state owes on past veterans' bonds.

faq.q: Hasn't California passed housing bonds before?
faq.a: Yes. Voters approved $2 billion in 2024 for housing people facing homelessness who have mental health or substance use challenges, including veterans. Voters also approved $1 billion for veterans' home loans in 2018.

label: Prop 2
title: Bigger rainy day fund
official: Increases State's Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Raise the cap on the state's main savings reserve from 10% to 20%.
what: Raises the cap on the state's [[rainy-day|Rainy Day Fund]] from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes and requires bigger deposits in years with unusually high capital gains revenue. It also extends required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040. Deposits would no longer count against the [[gann|state spending limit]] until they are withdrawn.
yes: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
no: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
fiscal: State budget reserves would be higher.
short_term: More money is set aside in good years, leaving less available to spend in those years.
long_term: Larger cushion for downturns. Because deposits stop counting against the spending limit, the state is less likely to hit that limit, which also affects when taxpayer rebates are triggered.
supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
opponents: None listed (argument against signed by Asm. David Tangipa, Sen. Steven Choi, and Carl DeMaio)
pro: Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
con: Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.
deep: Current rule (Prop 2 of 2014): deposit 0.75% of General Fund taxes yearly until the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes; above that, the money goes to infrastructure.
Prop 2 raises the ceiling to 20% and adds larger deposits when revenue from investment gains is very high.
Extends the required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and widens what they can cover, including amounts owed to schools and repayment of federal loans.
The spending-limit change is the main point of disagreement. Supporters see it as making saving possible; opponents see it as making rebates under the limit less likely.
The state currently holds about $20 billion in general-purpose reserves (California Today).

money.yesNote: No committee on either side has raised $1M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Does Prop 2 raise taxes or cut programs?
faq.a: It changes no taxes. It changes how much the state must save. In good years more money goes into savings, so less is available to spend that year. In a downturn there would be more savings to draw on, which the LAO says would make balancing the budget somewhat easier.

faq.q: How big would the rainy day fund get?
faq.a: Today the state must keep making deposits until the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes. Prop 2 raises that cap to 20%. It also requires larger deposits when taxes on investment gains are very high, such as during a stock market boom. The state now has about $20 billion in reserves it can use for any program.

faq.q: Could the state still use the money in an emergency?
faq.a: Today the state can stop deposits or withdraw money from the fund during a budget emergency. The LAO's description of Prop 2 does not list any change to that rule.

faq.q: Why does the spending limit part matter?
faq.a: Deposits into the rainy day fund would no longer count toward the [[gann|state spending limit]] until they are withdrawn. That makes the state less likely to hit the limit. Exceeding the limit is what triggers taxpayer rebates, which is the main point of disagreement. Supporters say the change makes saving possible. Opponents say it makes rebates less likely.

faq.q: What are the "extra debt payments"?
faq.a: Today the state must make extra payments toward state worker pension and retiree health debts through 2030. Each year's payment equals the amount first deposited into the rainy day fund. Prop 2 extends these payments to 2040. It also lets them cover more things, such as required payments to schools, repaying money borrowed from other state funds, and certain federal loans.

label: Prop 3
title: Keep high-income tax rates
official: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Make the 2012 income tax rates on top earners permanent instead of expiring.
what: Makes permanent the higher income tax rates on high earners that voters approved in 2012 (Prop 30) and extended in 2016 (Prop 55). They are now set to expire after the 2030 tax year.
yes: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
no: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
fiscal: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue after 2030.
short_term: No change to anyone's taxes before 2031. The rates in place today continue.
long_term: Keeps $5–15 billion a year that would otherwise be lost starting in 2031. Roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges.
supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
pro: PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
con: Californians already pay the nation's highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters' priorities. Don't reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.
deep: Rates (single filers; thresholds roughly double for joint filers, adjusted yearly for inflation): 10.3% on income from about $371,000 to $446,000; 11.3% from $446,000 to $743,000; 12.3% above $743,000. Without Prop 3, income above $371,000 would be taxed at 9.3% starting in 2031.
The LAO says the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates and pay about half of all state income taxes.
Revenue swings with the stock market because high earners' income depends heavily on capital gains, which is why the range is wide ($5–15 billion).
As a constitutional amendment, a future change would need another statewide vote.

money.yesNote: California Teachers Association $60M; National Education Association $7.5M; California School Employees Association $2.6M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Will my taxes go up?
faq.a: No one's tax rate goes up. Prop 3 keeps the current higher rates on high-income earners instead of letting them expire after the 2030 tax year. Only the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates.

faq.q: Who pays these rates?
faq.a: For a single filer, they apply to income above about $371,000 a year. The thresholds are roughly double for joint filers and are adjusted each year for inflation. The LAO says the top 2% of taxpayers who pay these rates also pay about half of all state income taxes.

faq.q: What happens if it fails?
faq.a: The higher rates expire, and starting in 2031 the top rate on income above those thresholds would fall to 9.3%. The state would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.

faq.q: Where does the money go?
faq.a: Roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges. The rest goes to other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.

faq.q: Why is the revenue estimate so wide?
faq.a: High earners' income depends heavily on the stock market, such as gains from selling stock. In a weak year the measure might bring in about $5 billion. In a strong year it might bring in $15 billion.

faq.q: Weren't these rates supposed to be temporary?
faq.a: Yes. Voters approved them as temporary in 2012 (Prop 30) and extended them in 2016 (Prop 55). Prop 3 would make them permanent. Because it is a [[ica|constitutional amendment]], changing them later would take another statewide vote.

label: Prop 4
title: Allow public campaign financing
official: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
short: Lift the 1988 ban so state and local governments may fund campaigns.
what: Repeals the 1988 law that bars the state, counties, and most cities from offering [[public-financing|public campaign financing]]. It does not create a program. Any government that wants one would have to set it up, within limits the measure sets.
yes: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
no: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
fiscal: A few hundred thousand dollars a year for the FPPC to advise governments. Any future program's cost depends on how it is designed.
short_term: Nothing changes until a government chooses to create a program.
long_term: Possible new programs at state or local level, each with its own cost, which the LAO says could be significant for governments that create one.
supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog
opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
pro: YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
con: Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.
deep: The current ban does not apply to [[charter-city|charter cities]]; Los Angeles, San Francisco, Oakland, Long Beach, and Berkeley already run programs.

Limits on any program: no money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety; no public funds for legal defense, fines, or repaying a candidate's personal loans; candidates must show broad support in their district and agree to spending limits.
The FPPC would issue guidance but would not be required to run local programs.
Also triples the maximum fine for campaign contributions from foreign entities.

money.yesNote: No committee on either side has raised $1M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Does Prop 4 spend tax money on campaigns?
faq.a: Not by itself. It lifts the ban on public campaign financing but does not create a program. The state, a county, or a city would have to set up its own program, within the limits Prop 4 sets.

faq.q: Could money for schools or police be used?
faq.a: No. Money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns.

faq.q: Who could receive public funds?
faq.a: Only candidates who show broad support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds could not pay for legal defense, fines, or repaying a candidate's personal loans to their own campaign.

faq.q: Do any California cities already do this?
faq.a: Yes. [[charter-city|Charter cities]] are exempt from the current ban. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley already provide public funds to some campaigns.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: The state would spend a few hundred thousand dollars a year for the [[fppc|FPPC]] to advise governments considering a program. The LAO says a future program's cost could be significant for any government that creates one, depending on its design.

label: Prop 5
title: Change how recalls work
official: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Remove the "who replaces them?" question from state recall ballots.
what: Removes the second question from state [[recall|recall elections]]. If an official is recalled, the vacancy would be filled by succession, appointment, or a later special election, depending on the office.
yes: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
no: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
fiscal: Net effect unknown. Each future recall could cost or save millions depending on the office.
short_term: No effect unless a recall qualifies.
long_term: A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor. Legislative seats would go to a special election; other statewide offices would be filled by the governor's appointment.
supporters: None submitted (argument in favor endorsed by League of Women Voters of CA and California Common Cause)
opponents: None submitted (argument against signed by Sen. Brian Jones and Asm. Joe Patterson)
pro: Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
con: Proposition 5 degrades California's century-old recall process by limiting voters' right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.
deep: A recalled governor would be replaced by the lieutenant governor, either until the next statewide election or, late in a term, for the rest of it.
A recalled official could run in the special election that follows.
Although the title says "statewide officers," the LAO notes the change also applies to legislative recalls.
Background: the 2003 governor recall drew 135 replacement candidates and the 2021 recall drew 46. Under today's rules a replacement can win with a plurality, without a majority.
The measure's author, former Sen. Josh Newman, was himself recalled in 2018.

money.yesNote: No committee on either side has raised $1M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Could voters still recall officials?
faq.a: Yes. Recalls would still happen the same way. Prop 5 only removes the second question, which asks who should replace the official if they are recalled.

faq.q: Who would replace a recalled governor?
faq.a: The lieutenant governor. If the recall happens in the first two years of the term, before the nomination period for the next statewide election closes, the lieutenant governor serves until voters elect a new governor at a later statewide election. If it happens later in the term, the lieutenant governor serves the rest of the term.

faq.q: What about legislators and other officials?
faq.a: A recalled legislator's seat would typically be filled by a special election. Other offices, such as attorney general or lieutenant governor, would be filled by the governor's appointment, as they are now when an office becomes vacant. Despite the measure's title, the LAO notes it covers legislators too.

faq.q: How does it work today?
faq.a: Voters answer both questions at once. If the official is recalled, whoever gets the most votes on the second question takes office, even without a majority. There were 135 replacement candidates in the 2003 governor recall and 46 in 2021.

faq.q: Would it save money?
faq.a: It depends on future recalls. A separate special election could cost millions. Dropping the replacement candidates from the ballot could save millions. The LAO says the net effect is unknown.

label: Prop 37
title: Loans for middle-income homebuyers
official: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
short: State-backed second loans so buyers of new homes can put 3% down.
what: Lets the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in [[revenue-bond|revenue bonds]] and lend eligible buyers up to 17% of a newly built home's price as a fixed-rate second loan. The buyer puts at least 3% down. Borrowers' payments repay the bonds.
yes: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
no: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
fiscal: No direct state or local costs.
short_term: A new loan program opens to buyers of qualifying new homes.
long_term: Unknown how much investors will buy the bonds and whether the program will lead to more homes being built (LAO).
supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma
pro: Zero Taxpayer Cost—No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
deep: Eligibility: California resident for at least a year, lives in the home, household income up to twice the [[ami|area median income]].
Home must be newly built (or the first sale of a converted nonresidential building) and priced under a county cap of roughly $1 million to $1.5 million.
The 17% loan is a second mortgage with monthly payments, not a grant.
Builders can opt into a "qualified builder option" that pairs higher labor standards with more flexible construction-defect rules.
Proponent is former Senate leader Robert Hertzberg.

money.yesNote: Realtor groups ~$20.0M (California Association of Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee $18.76M; National Association of Realtors $1.25M); Building a Better California $6M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Is the 17% help a grant?
faq.a: No. It is a loan covering up to 17% of the home price, which the buyer repays with monthly payments. Those payments repay the bonds and cover the program's costs.

faq.q: Who qualifies?
faq.a: California residents whose household income is no more than double the typical income in their area. The buyer must be the first purchaser of a newly built home, the price must be under set limits, and the buyer needs a down payment of at least 3%.

faq.q: Does it cost taxpayers?
faq.a: The LAO finds no direct state or local cost. These are [[revenue-bond|revenue bonds]], repaid by homebuyers' loan payments rather than the [[general-fund|General Fund]].

faq.q: Will it lead to more homes being built?
faq.a: The LAO says that is unknown. It depends on how many investors buy the bonds, how the loans compare in cost with other down payment programs, and whether builders and buyers respond.

faq.q: What is the "qualified builder option"?
faq.a: Builders can choose to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with certain training. In exchange they get more flexible construction-defect rules. Any builder's new homes can qualify for the loans, whether or not it chooses the option.

label: Prop 38
title: Immunology research bond
official: Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.
short: Borrow $8.4 billion for immune-system medical research.
what: Authorizes $8.4 billion in [[go-bond|general obligation bonds]] for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half goes to one University of California–affiliated nonprofit research institute and half to competitive research grants.
yes: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
no: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
fiscal: $500–600 million a year for about 20 years, with some or all of the cost offset if the research generates revenue.
short_term: Grants and institute funding begin as bonds are sold.
long_term: About $500–600 million a year from the General Fund for roughly 20 years. Any offset depends on research producing marketable treatments.
supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer's Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA
pro: YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer's. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love.
con: California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California's flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.
deep: At least $4.2 billion must go to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.
The single institute is chosen by the Department of Public Health; grant funds are awarded by a council of seven UC campuses and 10–15 other California institutions.
Treatments developed with the money must be sold in California at a 20% discount, and 10% of resulting revenue goes to the state until the bonds are repaid.

Proponent is Gary K. Michelson, whose entities account for about $66.2 million of the yes campaign's funds (FPPC, Oct 27). CalMatters reports the institute criteria currently match only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, of which he is the principal funder.
The "no cost to taxpayers" claim in the yes argument depends on future research revenue. The LAO's estimate is $500–600 million a year in repayment, possibly offset later.

money.yesNote: Gary Michelson and his Michelson Center for Public Policy $66.2M; Meyer Luskin $5M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Will Prop 38 raise my taxes?
faq.a: It creates no new tax. The state would repay the bonds from its [[general-fund|General Fund]], about $500–600 million a year for about 20 years. Because of interest, the total cost is about 10% more (after inflation) than paying up front.

faq.q: Who gets the money?
faq.a: About half goes to one research institute, selected by the Department of Public Health using criteria on size, funding, and ties to a UC campus. The other half becomes competitive grants, awarded by a council of 7 UC campuses and 10–15 other California research institutions to its own members. At least $4.2 billion must go to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.

faq.q: Is the institute share written for one institute?
faq.a: CalMatters reported that only one institute currently meets the criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. Its principal funder is Gary Michelson, who wrote Prop 38. The Department of Public Health would make the selection.

faq.q: Could the state get its money back?
faq.a: Possibly, in part. Ten percent of any revenue from discoveries goes to the state until the bond cost is repaid. The LAO says the amount could be significant but is uncertain, and repayment could take decades.

faq.q: What do Californians get besides research?
faq.a: Treatments developed with the money and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20% discount. Grant recipients must buy at least half their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.

faq.q: Has California funded medical research with bonds before?
faq.a: Yes. Voters approved $8.5 billion in stem cell research bonds through Prop 71 (2004) and Prop 14 (2020).

label: Prop 39
title: Voter ID and citizenship checks
official: Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Require government ID to vote in person and ID digits on mail ballots.
what: Requires government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, a voter must designate an ID in their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope; a mismatch means the ballot is not counted. Also requires officials to make "best efforts" to verify voters' citizenship.
yes: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
no: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
fiscal: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year to implement.
short_term: The Legislature must pass laws defining which IDs count and what "best efforts" means before full implementation.
long_term: Ongoing state and county costs. Fewer people may stay registered, from removal of ineligible voters or of eligible voters who lack ID; the LAO expects any savings from that to be smaller than the costs.
supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's Leadership Assn
opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
pro: Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
con: No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump's voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don't let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.
deep: How it works today: identity is established at registration with a driver's license number, state ID number, or last four of a Social Security number. In-person voters sign the roster; mail voters sign the envelope, and officials verify mail-ballot signatures before counting.
Scale: in November 2024 about 13 million of 16 million California voters used a [[vbm|mail ballot]].
Creates a free state voter ID card on request.
Officials must report each year the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship has been verified. The State Auditor reviews compliance every odd-numbered year.
U.S. citizenship is already required to register; falsely claiming it is perjury. San Francisco and Oakland allow certain noncitizen parents to vote only in school board elections.
As a constitutional amendment, the requirement would apply to every election in California, state and local.

money.yesNote: Richard Uihlein $17M; Joseph Gebbia $8M; Carl DeMaio's Reform California $3.1M
money.noNote: California Democratic Party ~$6.5M across three committees; California Nurses Association $2M; Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria $2M; Patty Quillin and Quinn Delaney $1.5M each; Reed Hastings $1M

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: What ID would I need?
faq.a: To vote in person, you would show a government-issued ID. To vote by mail, you would choose an ID in your voter registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope. The Legislature would still have to decide which IDs count.

faq.q: What if I don't have an ID?
faq.a: The state would have to provide a voter ID card free to anyone who asks for one.

faq.q: Can I still vote by mail?
faq.a: Yes. All registered voters get a mail ballot today, and the LAO does not describe Prop 39 changing that. You would need to select an ID in your registration, and officials would check that the ID digits on your envelope match your registration before counting your ballot.

faq.q: How is identity checked today?
faq.a: When you register, you give a driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. In-person voters sign the roster. Mail voters sign the envelope, and officials check that signature before counting the ballot. In November 2024, about 13 million of 16 million California voters voted by mail.

faq.q: Can noncitizens vote now?
faq.a: No, not in state or federal elections or almost any local election. Falsely claiming citizenship to register is perjury. The one exception: San Francisco and Oakland let certain noncitizen parents vote only in school board elections.

faq.q: When would it take effect, and what would it cost?
faq.a: The Legislature must first pass laws filling in details, such as which IDs count and what "best efforts" to verify citizenship means. The LAO estimates ongoing costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year. It would apply to every election in California, state and local.

label: Prop 40
title: One-time billionaire tax
official: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
short: A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California billionaires, mostly for health care.
what: Imposes a one-time [[wealth-tax|wealth tax]] of 5% of [[net-worth|net worth]] on people worth $1 billion or more who were California residents on January 1, 2026. Ninety percent of the money goes to health care; the rest to education, food assistance, and running the tax.
yes: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
no: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
fiscal: Temporary revenue of tens of billions of dollars over several years. Possible ongoing loss of less than $1 billion a year in income tax if some billionaires leave.
short_term: Tax due in 2027, or spread over five years at extra cost. Tens of billions of dollars for health care over several years.
long_term: Possible ongoing income tax loss of under $1 billion a year. The LAO says timing and amounts are very hard to predict because of stock prices and taxpayer responses.
supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
pro: Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It's time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
con: Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can't afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children's Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.
deep: Who pays: a few hundred Californians with net worth over $1 billion, many of whom built wealth in California technology companies.
What counts: businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property worldwide. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts are generally excluded.
Residency date of January 1, 2026 means moving away now does not avoid the tax. That backward-looking date is what Prop 42 calls a [[retroactive|retroactive tax]].
The revenue is exempt from the [[prop98|Prop 98 school guarantee]], reserve rules, and the [[gann|state spending limit]]. That exemption is the hook Prop 41 targets.
Administration could cost tens of millions of dollars a year for several years, paid from the tax revenue.
Governor Newsom and both candidates for governor oppose it, per the official argument against and the September 30 debate.
Read with Props 41 and 42: if either gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it. See Linked measures.

money.noNote: Main No committee $129.3M ($129.0M from Building a Better California); Golden State Promise $10.45M (Ripple Labs and Chris Larsen)

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Who would pay?
faq.a: Only people with a [[net-worth|net worth]] of $1 billion or more who were California residents on January 1, 2026. That is a few hundred people.

faq.q: Does it affect me if I'm not a billionaire?
faq.a: Not directly. The LAO says some billionaires might leave or otherwise reduce their income taxes, which could cost the state less than $1 billion a year in ongoing income tax revenue. That would leave less money in the [[general-fund|General Fund]] for other services.

faq.q: Can billionaires avoid it by moving?
faq.a: Not the tax itself, because it is based on residency on January 1, 2026. Moving away later could still reduce the state income taxes they would pay in future years.

faq.q: How much money, and where would it go?
faq.a: The LAO expects tens of billions of dollars over several years, but the timing and amount are very hard to predict. Ninety percent must go to health care, and the rest to education, food assistance, and running the tax. The money would not count toward the [[gann|state spending limit]] or the [[prop98|school funding guarantee]].

faq.q: What counts as wealth?
faq.a: Net worth: what a person owns, such as stocks, businesses, and other investments, minus debts. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts are generally excluded.

faq.q: Is it really one-time?
faq.a: Yes. The tax is due in 2027. Taxpayers can spread payments over five years but pay more to do so.

faq.q: What if Prop 40 and Prop 41 or 42 all pass?
faq.a: When measures passed at the same election [[conflict|conflict]], the one with the most yes votes generally wins. Props 41 and 42 are written to apply to taxes on this ballot. If either gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be blocked even if a majority approves it.
faq.src: California Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 10; LAO

label: Prop 41
title: Tax audits and spending-limit rule
official: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Audit programs funded by new special taxes; bar new taxes from escaping the spending limit.
what: Two parts. First, the State Auditor must review programs funded by any proposed new [[special-tax|special tax]] before a voter initiative reaches the ballot, and audit them every four years after. Second, no state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 may be excluded from the [[gann|state spending limit]], including taxes on this same ballot.
yes: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
no: The California State Auditor's responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
fiscal: Net effect unknown. Audit costs in the low millions of dollars a year, growing over time, mostly paid by new tax revenue.
short_term: Could stop Prop 40 if Prop 41 gets more yes votes. Audits start with the next special tax proposal.
long_term: Every new special tax gets a pre-ballot audit summary in the voter guide and four-year reviews. Future taxes could not be written to sit outside the spending limit.
supporters: CA Society of CPAs (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
pro: Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
con: Prop. 41 isn't really about audits—it's a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don't fall for the billionaires' lies. Vote NO on 41.
deep: The pre-ballot audit happens once supporters gather 25% of required signatures, before it is known whether the measure qualifies. It must identify ways to cut the program's annual cost by 10%.
If the measure fails or never reaches the ballot, the audit is paid from the General Fund; if it passes, from the new tax.
Audit summaries add pages to the voter guide, costing a few hundred thousand dollars per qualifying initiative.
The text does not name Prop 40, but it applies to taxes on the same ballot. Prop 40 exempts its revenue from the spending limit, which is the conflict the LAO flags.
The audits apply to state special taxes. Local special taxes are the subject of Prop 43.

money.noNote: No separate committee; opposed by the Yes on 40 campaign

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Does Prop 41 raise or cut any taxes?
faq.a: No. It adds audit requirements and changes how new taxes count toward the [[gann|state spending limit]].

faq.q: What would the audits do?
faq.a: When an initiative proposing a new state [[special-tax|special tax]] collects 25% of its needed signatures, the State Auditor would review the programs it would fund. The review must include ways to cut their yearly cost by 10%, and a summary would appear in the voter guide. Programs funded by special taxes created after January 1, 2026, by voters or the Legislature, would be audited every four years.

faq.q: Who pays for the audits?
faq.a: If the tax passes, the new tax revenue pays. If it fails or never reaches the ballot, the [[general-fund|General Fund]] pays. The LAO estimates the cost in the low millions of dollars a year, growing over time. Each audit summary would add a few hundred thousand dollars to the cost of printing and mailing the voter guide.

faq.q: Why is it linked to Prop 40?
faq.a: Prop 41 says no tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 can be excluded from the state spending limit, including taxes on this ballot. Prop 40 excludes its revenue from that limit. If Prop 41 gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be blocked.

faq.q: Does it apply to local taxes?
faq.a: Its audits cover state special taxes. Local special taxes are the subject of Prop 43.

label: Prop 42
title: Ban new taxes on what people own
official: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Constitutionally bar new state taxes on owning assets, and most retroactive taxes.
what: Bars any new state tax on owning [[personal-property|personal property]] (everything other than real estate, including stocks, retirement savings, business stakes, and digital assets). Also bars [[retroactive|retroactive taxes]], including ones based on where someone lived before the tax took effect. Applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, including on this ballot.
yes: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
no: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
fiscal: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
short_term: Could stop Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more yes votes.
long_term: A permanent constitutional limit on future tax options. The LAO says when and by how much revenues would be lower is unclear.
supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA
opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
pro: California's Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
con: This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn't really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
deep: Today: the state and local governments already tax some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and county taxes on business equipment. Those existing taxes are unaffected. Simply owning stocks or investment accounts is not taxed; income from them is.
Prop 40 is both a tax on owning assets (net worth) and keyed to a past residency date, so it falls under both prohibitions. That is why the LAO flags the conflict.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, a future wealth tax or similar would first need voters to amend the Constitution again.
At $146 million (as of October 27), Yes on 42 is the largest single committee on the ballot.

money.noNote: No separate committee; opposed by the Yes on 40 campaign

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Would this change any taxes I pay now?
faq.a: No. Existing taxes on personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and county taxes on business equipment, stay the same. Prop 42 bars new ones.

faq.q: Does it affect the property tax on my home?
faq.a: No. [[personal-property|Personal property]] means everything people own other than real estate.

faq.q: Would my stocks or retirement account be taxed?
faq.a: They are not taxed today just for owning them. The income they earn is. Prop 42 would prevent a new tax on simply owning them. Income from them would still be taxed as it is now.

faq.q: What is a retroactive tax?
faq.a: A tax that applies to things that happened in the past, such as a tax on money someone earned two years ago. Prop 42 limits when the Legislature or a ballot measure can impose one.

faq.q: How does it relate to Prop 40?
faq.a: Prop 40 taxes ownership of assets and is based on where someone lived on January 1, 2026, so it falls under both of Prop 42's bans. The official summary says Prop 42 nullifies conflicting taxes enacted after January 1, 2026. If Prop 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be blocked.

faq.q: Could it be changed later?
faq.a: It is a [[ica|constitutional amendment]], so changing it would take another statewide vote.

label: Prop 43
title: Two-thirds vote for citizen-proposed local taxes
official: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
short: Local special taxes proposed by voter petition would need two-thirds approval.
what: Local [[special-tax|special taxes]] placed on the ballot by a city council or board already need a [[two-thirds|two-thirds vote]]. Court rulings since 2017 let special taxes placed on the ballot by citizen petition pass with a simple majority. Starting January 1, 2027, Prop 43 would require two-thirds for those too.
yes: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
no: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
fiscal: Local government tax revenues may not go up as much in the future.
short_term: No effect on existing taxes. Applies to new, increased, or extended citizen-proposed special taxes from 2027.
long_term: Harder to pass voter-initiated local taxes for specific purposes, such as transit, housing, or schools. Actual effect depends on future local measures.
supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA
pro: Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13's two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
con: PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn't cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.
deep: Applies to cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.

The Legislature placed it on the ballot with near-unanimous votes (Senate 35–1, Assembly 68–2). News reports describe it as replacing a broader Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association initiative, which would also have affected some existing taxes.

Local angle: any future citizen-led special tax in Santa Clara County or San José would need two-thirds if this passes. It would not apply to the regional transit measure (RTM) on this ballot, because Prop 43 starts in 2027.
Unusual setup: a legislative measure whose listed supporters are taxpayer groups and whose listed opponents are public-employee unions.

money.yesNote: California Business Roundtable Issues PAC $10.24M; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association's Protect Prop. 13 $1.04M; Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett ($1M each)
money.noNote: Led by SEIU California ($1.5M), with firefighters', teachers', and building-trades unions

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Does it change any local taxes we already have?
faq.a: No. Starting January 1, 2027, it applies to new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters. A voter-proposed tax that is up for renewal after that date would need two-thirds.

faq.q: What is a special tax?
faq.a: A local tax dedicated to a specific purpose, such as transit, parks, or housing. Prop 43 does not affect general taxes, which can be spent on anything.

faq.q: What is the rule today?
faq.a: Special taxes placed on the ballot by a city council or board already need a [[two-thirds|two-thirds vote]]. Recent court decisions let special taxes proposed by voters through petitions pass with a simple majority. Prop 43 would require two-thirds for those as well.

faq.q: Does it affect Measure RTM on my ballot?
faq.a: No. Prop 43 does not start until January 1, 2027, so it does not change the vote needed for anything on this ballot.

faq.q: Who put it on the ballot?
faq.a: The Legislature, by a near-unanimous vote. News reports describe it as replacing a broader Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association initiative that would also have affected some existing taxes.

label: Prop 44
title: 90% spending rule for community clinics
official: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
short: Nonprofit community clinics must spend 90% of revenue on services or pay a penalty.
what: Requires private nonprofit [[fqhc|Federally Qualified Health Centers]] to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on "program services." The Attorney General defines that term. Clinics that fall short pay the gap to the state as a penalty, refundable if they comply within five years.
yes: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
no: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
fiscal: State costs in the low tens of millions of dollars a year, covered by fees on clinics.
short_term: The Attorney General writes rules defining "program services"; clinics adjust spending.
long_term: The LAO says clinics currently report spending about 80% of revenue on health care services on average, and some that cannot meet 90% might close.
opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
pro: Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics' charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
con: Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44!
deep: California has about 2,000 safety-net clinics (LAO).
The definition of "program services" matters a great deal. The measure says it includes but is not limited to patient services; the final line will be set in Attorney General rulemaking.
Unrefunded penalties go to clinic workforce programs.
The same union, SEIU-UHW, sponsors Prop 40. News reports say a similar bill (AB 1113) died in the Legislature.
yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Which clinics does it cover?
faq.a: Private nonprofit safety-net clinics, which mainly serve low-income and uninsured patients. California has about 2,000 safety-net clinics, and most are private nonprofits. Clinics run by counties and other public agencies are not covered.

faq.q: How much do clinics spend on care now?
faq.a: On average, about 80% of their revenue goes to health care services, though it varies by clinic. Prop 44 would require at least 90%.

faq.q: What counts as health care spending?
faq.a: The Attorney General would decide, starting from the reports clinics already file with the federal government. That definition will determine how many clinics already meet the 90% rule.

faq.q: What if a clinic falls short?
faq.a: It pays the state the amount of the shortfall as a penalty. It gets the money back if it complies within five years. If not, the money goes to clinic workforce programs. Clinics can ask for a temporary waiver in some cases.

faq.q: Could clinics close?
faq.a: The LAO says some clinics that cannot meet the requirement might close. Others might spend more on patient care, which could raise state Medi-Cal costs. The state would spend low tens of millions of dollars a year on enforcement, paid by fees on clinics.

label: Prop 45
title: Faster environmental review
official: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
short: An optional fast track through CEQA for housing, water, energy, and other projects.
what: Creates an optional, faster path through [[ceqa|CEQA]] for nine kinds of "essential" projects: housing, water systems, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, schools, and transportation. It sets binding deadlines and narrows what courts can stop.
yes: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
no: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
fiscal: Initial state and local costs in the high tens of millions of dollars a year, possibly over $100 million, partly covered by fees. Longer-term effects uncertain and potentially larger, in either direction.
short_term: Agencies set up new procedures; applicants choose between the new track and existing law.
long_term: Could speed approval of covered projects. The LAO says long-term fiscal effects could be significant, positive or negative.
supporters: California Children's Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing
opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
pro: The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California's strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California.
con: PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won't lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.
deep: Key changes on the fast track: a 365-business-day limit to finish an [[eir|environmental impact report]]; the applicant may propose a single alternative instead of the agency developing several; standards are frozen at the date of application; public comment periods are capped; tribal consultation is limited to federally recognized tribes.
Courts could no longer halt an entire project over a CEQA violation, only the deficient part while the agency fixes it.
Exclusions: Delta water conveyance, nuclear energy, and high-speed rail are not eligible.
Proponent attorney Kurt Oneto also filed Props 41 and 42.

money.yesNote: Building a Better California $10M; California Building Industry Association and its committee ~$10.6M; CA Business PAC $3.9M; PG&E $2.4M; Edison International $2M
money.noNote: Wendy Schmidt $10M; Clean and Healthy California $7.1M; building trades, laborers', and iron workers' unions

yesNoSrc: "What your vote means," Official Voter Information Guide.

faq.q: Does Prop 45 get rid of CEQA?
faq.a: No. It creates an optional faster track through [[ceqa|CEQA]] for certain "essential" projects. Applicants can use the new process or the existing one.

faq.q: Which projects qualify?
faq.a: Nine categories: housing, water systems, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, schools, and transportation. Delta water conveyance, nuclear energy, and high-speed rail are excluded.

faq.q: What would change in the review?
faq.a: There would be a 365-business-day limit to finish an [[eir|environmental impact report]], and impacts would be judged by the standards in place when the application is filed. The applicant could propose a single alternative instead of the agency developing several. Public comment periods would have a maximum length, and tribal consultation would be limited to federally recognized tribes.

faq.q: Could people still sue?
faq.a: Yes, but courts could consider less, and lawsuits would face time limits. A court could stop only the part of a project with a flawed review, not the whole project, while the agency fixes it.

faq.q: What would it cost?
faq.a: The LAO estimates state and local costs in the high tens of millions of dollars a year at first, possibly over $100 million, partly covered by fees. Longer-term effects are uncertain but could be larger. Faster projects could lower costs and raise tax revenue, while approving projects with harmful environmental effects could create new costs.
